source.title: Legal-Tech Open Diaries: Lesson learned on how to develop and deploy light-weight models in the era of humongous Language Models
source.authors: Stelios Maroudas; Sotiris Legkas; Prodromos Malakasiotis; Ilias Chalkidis

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some table and appendix formatting is flattened, but the relevant values are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares pretraining validation loss across differently sized models and downstream benchmark scores across model sizes, but does not fit or test the original scaling-law equations.
record.gate_note: The paper reports overall and per-language MLM validation cross-entropy, a pretraining-loss figure, and downstream task scores by model size. It does not fit power laws, test small-run extrapolation, or search for compute-optimal allocations. The rows below retain the overall validation-loss values and one principal downstream metric per task; per-language MLM results and secondary downstream metrics are not included.
record.test_reason: In a new setting (multilingual legal-domain MLM), the paper trains four C-XLM sizes (9M–368M) on the same 92B tokens. It reports held-out MLM cross-entropy (Table 15) and fine-tuned scores on five tasks (Table 2) by size. These results bear weakly on V1 (loss falls with parameters) and V6 (downstream improves with scale). There are no power-law fits, no token or compute sweeps and no extrapolation, and model shape co-varies with size.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that larger models outperform smaller ones, with gains varying by task. They also conclude that domain-specific models outperform generic ones, though the gap narrows for large models. Their main contribution is that fully compressed models (pruned, distilled, quantized) beat equally sized fine-tuned or distilled models: about 42× smaller and 66× faster for a 2.3 p.p. loss.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains multilingual legal-domain masked-language models and compares several sizes; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law fitting or compute-optimal allocation procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream performance varies across tasks; the paper also reports language-dependent differences in downstream performance.
record.problems: Only a small number of model sizes are evaluated, and model size changes jointly with depth, width, and number of heads. The study does not fit power laws or report uncertainty for the listed scores. C-XLM and XLM-R also differ in vocabulary, training data, and training-token volume.
record.rows_left_out: Table 15 reports additional MLM validation-loss results by language and corpus subset; these were omitted in favor of the overall values to stay within the row limit. Table 2 reports secondary downstream metrics (m-F1 and UNFAIR-ToS MAE), and Appendix Tables 12–14 provide per-language or compression-step results; these are not included here.

untested.parts: Power-law form and fit; behaviour over several orders of magnitude (only ~1.6 decades in parameters); token and compute scaling (tokens fixed at 92B).
All; no small-run fits are used to predict larger runs.
All; no fixed-compute allocation sweep (the authors only invoke Hoffmann et al. to argue their models are not under-trained).
All; depth, width and heads are halved together with size, never varied at fixed parameter count.
All; the paper covers text MLM pretraining only. Fine-tuned scores are not fitted to a scaling form.
Predictability, i.e. any fitted relation between downstream score and scale or pretraining loss.
All; no fitting choices are compared.

missing.what: The authors state that per-language MLM accuracy does not correlate with per-language downstream performance. This bears on V6 predictability from pretraining loss, but no statistic is given.
Secondary-metric reversals for XLM-R base→large: Obligations m-F1 88.2→87.4; ContractNER m-F1 93.9→93.7.
Pre-training loss curves for the four C-XLM sizes over training steps (a tokens/steps dimension). Shown only as a figure, with no values.

record.verdict_notes: This is primarily a legal-tech engineering and compression paper; the scaling evidence is incidental. The four sizes co-vary depth, width and heads, so shape effects are confounded with size. C-XLM and XLM-R differ in data, vocabulary and tokens (63× more for XLM-R), so cross-family rows should not be read as scale comparisons. The flattening of C-XLM loss at 368M under fixed steps is worth noting, but it is not analysed by the authors. No uncertainty is reported anywhere.

versions.untested_parts: The paper compares validation loss across a few model sizes, but does not fit a power law, establish behavior over several orders of magnitude, or sweep training tokens and compute.
No fits on small runs are used to predict much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token trend is evaluated.
Depth, width, and other architecture details are not varied at fixed parameter count.
The experiments concern text MLM pretraining and legal downstream tasks; other modalities and the listed training regimes are not tested.
The paper reports downstream scores at different sizes but does not fit a predictive relationship between downstream performance and scale or pretraining loss.
The paper does not compare scaling-law fitting choices or estimate competing exponents.

rows.check: Loss still falls (1.03→0.90), but the local log-log slope drops sharply: about −0.52 (tiny→small), −0.33 (small→base), −0.08 (base→large). Over this 1.6-decade range the curve bends rather than following a single pure power law. An irreducible-loss term or the fixed 1.1M-step schedule could explain this; the paper does not analyse it.

relationships.condition: C-XLM tiny→large (9M–368M parameters, fixed 92B tokens), overall held-out legal MLM loss
relationships.reason: Validation cross-entropy falls monotonically from 2.37 to 1.53, 1.03 and 0.90 with parameters (mlm-cxt, mlm-cxs, mlm-cxb, mlm-cxl). The decrease is consistent with V1, but the gain shrinks sharply at the top and no power law is fitted.
relationships.display_finding: Validation cross-entropy decreased from 2.37 to 1.53, 1.03 and 0.90 as parameters increased, with sharply smaller final gains and no fitted power law.

relationships.condition: C-XLM size sequence, all five downstream tasks, principal metric
relationships.reason: Scores rise at every C-XLM size step on MultiEURLEX, UNFAIR-ToS, CNLI, Obligations and ContractNER (down-*-cxt/cxs/cxb/cxl). Gains shrink at larger sizes on some tasks, e.g. ContractNER 92.9→93.2.
relationships.display_finding: Scores increased at every size step on all five tasks, with shrinking gains on some tasks, including ContractNER from 92.9 to 93.2.

relationships.condition: XLM-R base vs large on Contract-Obligations
relationships.reason: The larger XLM-R scores lower, 88.9 vs 89.7 µ-F1 (down-oblig-xrb, down-oblig-xrl). m-F1 is also lower, and ContractNER m-F1 is lower too (93.7 vs 93.9; not in rows). The gaps are small and no uncertainty is reported.
relationships.display_finding: Contract-Obligations micro-F1 falls from 89.7 to 88.9 and macro-F1 also declines, while ContractNER macro-F1 falls from 93.9 to 93.7, with uncertainty unreported.

relationships.condition: Per-language downstream performance vs per-language MLM accuracy (C-XLM)
relationships.reason: Based on the text, not rows: the authors state that pretraining MLM accuracy across languages does not correlate with downstream performance. No correlation number is given.
relationships.display_finding: Pretraining masked-language-model accuracy across languages reportedly does not correlate with downstream performance.
